line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 g3
teaches: A fianchetto is unusual in the open game, and that is most of its value at club level: the resulting positions are sound but unfamiliar, so the opponent is out of book while nothing has been risked. It is reachable through more than one move order, which makes it hard to sidestep — the knights can come out in either order before the g-pawn moves.
explains: Both knights are developed and the g-pawn steps forward to put the bishop on the long diagonal rather than on the usual c4 or b5 square. Nothing is committed yet in the centre: the plan waits to see which setup Black chooses, because the pawn structure Black picks decides where White's pieces belong.
structural: why an unusual-but-sound setup is worth playing at club level
